summary.text: Writing \(p=2t+1\), Lucas congruences pair the \(k\) and \(p+k\) summands to show both relevant values at \(p+m\) vanish modulo \(p\) for \(0\le m<p-1\), while at \(p-1\) the two anti-diagonal values are respectively \(1\) and \((-1)^t\) (in the latter case all terms except \(k=t\) vanish). Thus both Hankel matrices are anti-triangular modulo \(p\); multiplying their constant anti-diagonal entries and the reversal sign \((-1)^t\) gives the two claimed determinant residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                 \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and write
\[
p=2t+1,
\qquad t=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\), or equivalently identities in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We first establish the binomial-coefficient congruences needed in the proof.

By Lucas's theorem, if the base-\(p\) expansions of \(N\) and \(K\) have digits \(N_i\) and \(K_i\), then
\[
\binom NK\equiv\prod_i\binom{N_i}{K_i}\pmod p.
\]
For the small numbers occurring here, this gives, whenever \(m,k<p\),
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk,
\qquad
\binom{p+m}{p+k}\equiv\binom mk. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the base-\(p\) digits of \(p+m\) are \((1,m)\); the digits of \(k\) are \((0,k)\), while those of \(p+k\) are \((1,k)\).

We will also use the following vanishing of central binomial coefficients:
\[
k<p,\quad p\leq 2k
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0. \tag{2}
\]
To see this, write \(2k=p+d\), where \(0\leq d<p\). Since \(k<p\), Lucas's theorem gives
\[
\binom{2k}{k}=\binom{p+d}{k}
 \equiv \binom10\binom dk.
\]
But \(d=2k-p<k\), so \(\binom dk=0\).

A second central-binomial congruence, valid for \(0\leq j<p\), is
\[
\binom{2(p+j)}{p+j}\equiv 2\binom{2j}{j}. \tag{3}
\]
Here is a direct coefficient proof. In \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), the Frobenius identity gives
\[
(1+x)^p=1+x^p.
\]
Consequently
\[
(1+x)^{2(p+j)}=(1+x^p)^2(1+x)^{2j}
=(1+2x^p+x^{2p})(1+x)^{2j}.
\]
The coefficient of \(x^{p+j}\) on the left is
\(\binom{2(p+j)}{p+j}\). On the right, the term \(2x^p\) contributes
\(2\binom{2j}{j}\). The constant term of \(1+2x^p+x^{2p}\) would require the coefficient of \(x^{p+j}\) in \((1+x)^{2j}\), which is zero because \(p+j>2j\) when \(j<p\). The term \(x^{2p}\) cannot contribute either, since it would require degree \(j-p<0\). This proves (3).

Finally, for \(0\leq k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k. \tag{4}
\]
For example, this follows from
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
 =\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
 \equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k,
\]
where \(k!\) is invertible modulo \(p\). (For \(k=0\), both sides are \(1\).)

We next determine the values needed from \(a(n)\).

First,
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, by (4),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p=2t+1\), this last sum has \(2t+1\) terms and equals \(1\): the terms with indices \(2r\) and \(2r+1\) cancel for \(0\leq r<t\), leaving the final term \((-1)^{2t}=1\).

We also claim that, for every integer \(m\) satisfying
\[
0\leq m<p-1,
\]
one has
\[
a(p+m)\equiv0. \tag{6}
\]
Split the defining sum into the three ranges
\[
0\leq k\leq m,
\qquad m<k<p,
\qquad p\leq k\leq p+m.
\]
In the middle range, (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk=0,
\]
because \(k>m\). Thus every middle-range summand vanishes.

The terms in the first and third ranges cancel in pairs. Pair the index \(k\), where \(0\leq k\leq m\), with \(p+k\). By (1),
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{p+m}{p+k}\equiv\binom mk.
\]
Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+k}=-(-1)^k.
\]
Therefore
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p+m}{k}^4
+
(-1)^{p+k}\binom{p+m}{p+k}^4
\equiv0.
\]
This proves (6).

We now establish the analogous facts about \(c(n)\). First,
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^t. \tag{7}
\]
Consider a summand indexed by \(k\), with \(0\leq k<p\). If \(k<t\), put
\(r=p-1-k\). Then \(r<p\), and
\[
2r=2(p-1-k)\geq p;
\]
indeed, the smallest possible value in this case occurs at \(k=t-1\), when \(r=t+1\) and \(2r=p+1\). Hence (2) shows
\[
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}=\binom{2r}{r}\equiv0.
\]
Thus all terms with \(k<t\) vanish. If \(k>t\), then \(2k\geq2(t+1)=p+1\), so (2) gives
\[
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0.
\]
Thus all terms with \(k>t\) vanish as well. Only \(k=t\) remains.

For \(k=t\), since \(p-1=2t\), we have \(p-1-t=t\), and every binomial coefficient in this summand is \(\binom{p-1}{t}\). By (4), it is congruent to \((-1)^t\). Therefore the surviving term is
\[
(-1)^t
 \binom{p-1}{t}^{2}
 \binom{2t}{t}
 \binom{2t}{t}
\equiv
(-1)^t\bigl((-1)^t\bigr)^4
=(-1)^{5t}=(-1)^t.
\]
This proves (7).

Next we claim that for every \(m\) with \(0\leq m<p-1\),
\[
c(p+m)\equiv0. \tag{8}
\]
As in the proof for \(a\), divide the indices into
\[
0\leq k\leq m,
\qquad m<k<p,
\qquad p\leq k\leq p+m.
\]
For \(m<k<p\), formula (1) gives
\(\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk=0\), so the entire summand vanishes.

It remains to pair the term at \(k\), for \(0\leq k\leq m\), with the term at \(p+k\). Set
\[
r=m-k.
\]
Then \(0\leq r<p\). For the term at \(k\), (1) and (3) give
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk

a nd
\binom{2(p+m-k)}{p+m-k}
=\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}
\equiv2\binom{2r}{r}.
\]
Thus the term at \(k\) is congruent to
\[
2(-1)^k\binom mk^2\binom{2k}{k}\binom{2r}{r}. \tag{9}
\]
For the paired index \(p+k\), we have
\[
p+m-(p+k)=m-k=r.
\]
Using (1) and (3) again,
\[
\binom{p+m}{p+k}\equiv\binom mk,
\qquad
\binom{2(p+k)}{p+k}\equiv2\binom{2k}{k}.
\]
The remaining central binomial coefficient is simply \(\binom{2r}{r}\). Since \((-1)^{p+k}=-(-1)^k\), the term at \(p+k\) is congruent to
\[
-2(-1)^k\binom mk^2\binom{2k}{k}\binom{2r}{r}, \tag{10}
\]
which is the negative of (9). Every first-range term therefore cancels with its paired third-range term. This proves (8).

We now turn to the determinant reduction. We use the following elementary anti-triangular determinant fact. Let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\leq i,j<p}\) be a matrix over any commutative ring such that
\[
M_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }i+j\geq p.
\]
Then
\[
\det M=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{i,p-1-i}, \tag{11}
\]
where \(\rho(j)=p-1-j\) is the reversal permutation.

Indeed, reverse the order of the columns. The resulting matrix \(N\) has entries
\[
N_{ij}=M_{i,p-1-j}.
\]
If \(i>j\), then
\[
i+(p-1-j)\geq p,
\]
so \(N_{ij}=0\). Hence \(N\) is upper triangular and
\[
\det N=\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}N_{ii}
      =\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{i,p-1-i}.
\]
On the other hand, reversing the columns multiplies the determinant by
\(\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\). Since this sign is its own inverse, (11) follows.

The reversal permutation has one inversion for every pair of distinct indices, so
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
For \(p=2t+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=t(2t+1)=t+2t^2,
\]
which has the same parity as \(t\). Consequently
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^t. \tag{12}
\]
Thus, if all the entries on the anti-diagonal of \(M\) are equal to a common value \(d\), (11) and (12) yield
\[
\det M=(-1)^t d^p. \tag{13}
\]

Apply this first to the Hankel matrix
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p},
\]
viewed modulo \(p\). If \(i+j\geq p\), then, because \(i,j\leq p-1\), we may write
\[
i+j=p+m,
\qquad 0\leq m\leq p-2.
\]
Equation (6) therefore gives \(a(i+j)\equiv0\). Thus \(A\) satisfies the anti-triangular hypothesis. On its anti-diagonal, \(j=p-1-i\), so
\[
i+j=p-1,
\]
and (5) gives
\[
a(i+j)=a(p-1)\equiv1.
\]
Taking \(d=1\) in (13), we obtain
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^t=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p. \tag{14}
\]

Finally apply the same argument to
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}.
\]
Whenever \(i+j\geq p\), write again \(i+j=p+m\) with \(0\leq m\leq p-2\). Equation (8) gives \(c(i+j)\equiv0\). Every anti-diagonal entry equals, by (7),
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^t.
\]
Formula (13), now with \(d=(-1)^t\), gives
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^t\bigl((-1)^t\bigr)^p.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(\bigl((-1)^t\bigr)^p=(-1)^t\). Hence
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^t(-1)^t=(-1)^{2t}=1\pmod p. \tag{15}
\]

Equations (14) and (15) are precisely the two asserted determinant congruences.
